subtopic: Moving to a new city for study
subtype: Approach: asking for help when homesickness lingers [Revision]
passage: Two months in, I stopped being able to sleep. I lay awake till three, then dragged myself to class with a heavy head, and I stopped laughing at anything. I told myself it was just homesickness and kept quiet. Then Alka ma'am, our warden, asked, “Beti, when did you last eat properly with someone?” and I cried in her office. She listened and took me to the college counsellor the next morning. They didn't hand me a magic fix. They asked questions and we made a plan: talk once a week, join the Saturday photography club, and a trip back home when term ends. The club was awkward at first. I'm Kavitha, and I'm sleeping a bit better now, and I know the ticket home is booked.

qa.a: Kavitha joined the Saturday photography club.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling in the warden's office?
qa.a: Kavitha felt overwhelmed and sad, since she cried when the warden asked a caring question after weeks of keeping quiet.

qa.q: What could Kavitha do if she still feels low after the term break?
qa.a: She could keep meeting the counsellor and tell the warden or her family, since a low mood that keeps going is something to keep sharing with support.

qa.q: How might the warden see Kavitha coming in?
qa.a: Alka ma'am probably felt concerned and glad that Kavitha opened up, since she asked a caring question and acted the next morning.

grounding: After two months of poor sleep and low mood, a teen speaks to the warden and a counsellor, joins a weekend club and plans a visit home.

subtopic: Moving to a new city for study
subtype: Approach: asking for help when homesickness lingers [Revision]
passage:
I'm Sarita, and my room is across the corridor from Bhupen's in our college hostel. For his first two months, his light was on at two and three in the morning. He stopped coming to the mess on weekends. When I asked how he was, he always said, “Fine, just tired.”
In the ninth week I saw him knock on the warden's door after dinner and go in for a long time. The next Tuesday he was in the counsellor's waiting room when I went in for my scholarship form.
Things changed slowly after that. On Saturday mornings he started leaving early with the photography club, camera round his neck. His light went off earlier. He told me once that he'd booked a train home for the Diwali break and was counting the weeks, but in a good way.
I don't know what he said to the warden. But I think asking was the hard part.

qa.q: Which club did Bhupen start going out with on Saturdays?
What might Bhupen have been feeling during those first two months?
qa.a: Bhupen was probably homesick and low, sleeping badly while telling people he was fine.

qa.q: What else could help Bhupen while waiting for the Diwali break?
qa.a: Keep seeing the counsellor and set regular calls home, so the weeks feel manageable.

qa.q: How does the change look to Sarita?
qa.a: Sarita sees the late lights and missed meals give way to a busier, calmer Bhupen, and senses that asking for help was the hard part.

grounding: A hostel neighbour sees a teen who has slept badly and felt low for two months go to the warden and counsellor, join a weekend club and plan a trip home.

subtopic: Moving to a new city for study
subtype: Approach: asking for help when homesickness lingers [Revision]
passage:
Week eight, Sunday night: Francis hasn't slept properly in weeks. He hasn't gone out with anyone since September. He lies on his hostel bed in Chennai scrolling through photos of home in Shillong. He tells himself it will pass on its own. It hasn't.
Week nine, Monday: He knocks on the warden's door. “Sir, I'm not doing well. I miss home all the time.” The warden listens, then walks him to the college counsellor's office and books a slot for Thursday. The counsellor suggests one thing to look forward to every week.
Week nine, Saturday: Francis joins the Saturday football group that Kishore, from his floor, has invited him to three times. He's out of breath and laughing by the end.
Week ten: He books a train home for the term break and pins the ticket above his desk. He sleeps through most nights now.

qa.q: How many times had Kishore invited Francis to football?
What was Francis feeling on the Sunday night of week eight?
qa.a: Francis felt homesick and low, and hoping it would fade on its own had not worked.

qa.q: What else could Francis add if the homesickness returns?
qa.a: Go back to the counsellor, and keep one weekly thing to look forward to, like the football.

qa.q: How might Kishore feel when Francis finally joins?
qa.a: Kishore probably feels glad that the invitations paid off and a floor-mate is finally joining in.

grounding: Shows a teen who has slept poorly and felt low for two months speaking to the warden and counsellor, joining a weekend group, and booking a trip home for the break.
